targets.title: Studies of interference in serial verbal reactions.
targets.evidence_quote: In the Stroop task (Stroop, 1935), participants view words one at a time in different colors. Participants categorize the color of the font and do not need to do anything with the meaning of the word.
targets.outcome_quote: Across the replication studies (N = 3,279), participants took longer to categorize incongruent words than congruent words (M = 0.27, SD = 0.31), t(3,336) = 50.22, p < .001, d = .88, 95% CI = [.84, .92]. This replicated the basic effect from previous research.

targets.title: Metaphoric structuring: Understanding time through spatial metaphors.
targets.evidence_quote: Boroditsky (2000) demonstrated that priming participants with an ego-moving or object- moving frame of reference can influence their interpretation of an ambiguous temporal statement.
targets.outcome_quote: The effect size was weaker, and the condition differences were shifted toward selecting Friday, compared to the original study, but the replications were nonetheless consistent with the key feature of the original demonstration: object-priming increased the likelihood of selecting Monday compared to Friday.

targets.title: Availability: A heuristic for judging frequency and probability.
targets.evidence_quote: Tversky and Kahneman (1973) examined whether undergraduates recruited separately from a participant pool would overestimate the frequency of easier-to-imagine words relative to harder-to-imagine words.
targets.outcome_quote: Across the replication studies (N = 3,088), 1,612/3,088 participants judged the first position to be more frequent for the majority of letters and 1,476/3,088 judged the third position to be more frequent for the majority of letters. The probability of favoring the first position was weak but reliable, PSdep = 0.522, p = .015, d = .09, 95% CI = [.02, .16].
targets.outcome_reasoning: Primary aggregate bias and ratio estimate agree with the original. Letterwise tests are explicitly exploratory.

targets.authors: De Fruyt, Van De Wiele, & Van Heeringen
targets.evidence_quote: De Fruyt and colleagues (2000) investigated the relation between Cloninger’s Temperament and Character Dimensions (Cloninger, 1987) and the Big Five personality index. The researchers found that Cloninger-assessed persistence correlated with the Big Five trait conscientiousness, r(128) = .46, p < .001, d = 1.04, 95% CI = [.64, 1.43].
targets.outcome_quote: Across all replication studies (N = 3,193), there was little evidence for a relationship between conscientiousness measured with the TIPI and persistence measured with the unsolvable anagram task, r(3191) = .027, p = .134, 95% CI = [-0.008, 0.061], d = .05, 95% CI = [-.02, .12].
targets.outcome_reasoning: No De Fruyt entry appears in the supplied reference list; author names and year are supplied by the effect heading, title and DOI unavailable. Behavioral conceptual replication has no reliable predicted correlation.

targets.authors: Galinsky, A. D., Magee, J. C., Inesi, M. E., & Gruenfeld, D. H.
targets.title: Power and perspectives not taken.
targets.evidence_quote: Galinsky et al. (2006) examined whether power can impair perspective taking. Their Study 2a tested whether individuals made to feel high in power were more likely to inaccurately assume that others perceive the world from the same perspective as they do compared to those made to feel low in power.
targets.outcome_quote: In sum, the replications did not provide evidence of an effect of power on perspective taking.

targets.evidence_quote: Cacioppo and colleagues (1983) investigated the impact of argument strength on persuasion, inviting participants who scored in the upper or lower third on the Need for Cognition Scale (Cacioppo & Petty, 1982) to participate.
targets.outcome_quote: Finally, in Elaboration Likelihood (Cacioppo et al., 1983), we observed that stronger arguments were more persuasive than weaker arguments, but this was not qualified by need for cognition.

targets.title: It feels like yesterday: Self-esteem, valence of personal past experiences, and judgments of subjective distance.
targets.evidence_quote: Ross and Wilson (2002) examined how subjective temporal distance varies when recalling negative compared to positive events and whether differences in self-esteem may be associated with how distant events subjectively feel, irrespective of how distant they actually are.
targets.outcome_quote: Likewise, for Self-Esteem and Subjective Distance (Ross & Wilson, 2002), we did observe that positive past events felt closer than negative past events, but we did not replicate the moderation of this effect by self-esteem.

targets.title: Moral credentials and the expression of prejudice.
targets.evidence_quote: Monin and Miller (2001) tested whether participants were more willing to express prejudicial attitudes when their prior behavior provided evidence that they were non-prejudiced.
targets.outcome_quote: In sum, the replications showed a similar main effect of the predicted credentials manipulation on making sexist judgments, but did not replicate the unexpected moderation by gender.14

targets.title: Some participants may be better than others: Sustained attention and motivation are higher early in semester.
targets.evidence_quote: The present study replicated and extended prior observations (Nicholls et al., 2014; Witt et al., 2011). As the semester progressed, participants reported slightly less effort and attention, were slightly more likely to fail an attention check, were slightly less conscientious, had slightly worse mood, had slightly higher stress, and had slightly higher representation of men compared to women.
